title: Water: where it is, how it goes round, and how it shapes land and life
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 5 'Water — The Essence of Life' (forms and sources of water, fresh and salt; uses; the water cycle; water shaping land; freshwater habitats; conservation). No textbook needed.
summary: Only a tiny part of Earth's water is fresh water we can reach, and the same water keeps going round and round. Your child shows this with a bucket and a teaspoon, makes salt from salty water, watches drops form on a cold glass, builds a water cycle in a bag, catches water leaving a plant's leaves, tests which ground soaks up rain, makes a river in a tray, and finds out how pond plants and animals live in water. It ends with a model house that catches its own rain.
builds_on: Class 3 water rung: rain soaks in, runs off or evaporates; groundwater fills wells; a matka cools by evaporation; clear is not clean; water is shared. This rung adds condensation, transpiration, the full water cycle, fresh and salt water, how rivers carve land and where they drain, freshwater habitats, and how communities catch and share water. Later (middle school): water as a solvent, the science of clouds and monsoons, and water treatment.
goals: By the end your child can show how little of Earth's water is fresh and easy to reach, and why sea water can't simply be drunk.
By the end your child can name the three forms of water and the changes between them: melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation.
By the end your child can draw and explain the water cycle, including transpiration from plants and water soaking into the ground.
By the end your child can show how flowing water wears away land and builds new land, and say which sea their local rain ends up in.
By the end your child can describe a freshwater habitat and a pond food chain, and explain how one water plant or animal is suited to their home.
By the end your child can explain how villages catch and share water, and argue about who a river belongs to.
subconcepts: three forms of water: ice, liquid and vapour
salt water and fresh water: how little is fresh and reachable
clouds are tiny drops formed on specks of dust, not vapour
the water cycle has no start or end
transpiration: plants put water into the air
water shapes land: erosion and deposition, valleys and deltas
river basins: which sea our rain flows to
freshwater habitats and pond food chains
adaptations for life in water: lotus leaf, water strider, fish gills
catching and sharing water: johads, rain harvesting, water budgets
hidden water in food and things
words: water as an invisible gas in the air
liquid water turning into water vapour
water vapour cooling and turning back into tiny drops of liquid
water falling from clouds as rain, hail or snow
water leaving a plant as vapour through tiny holes in the leaves
water soaking down into the ground
refilling groundwater with rain that soaks in

days.title: All the water in the world
days.goal: Climb up from Class 3, meet the story, and see how little of Earth's water we can use.

steps.title: What do we already know?
steps.do: Recall the Class 3 water lesson in one quick round. Ask: 'When rain lands, what three things can happen to it?' (It soaks in, runs off, or evaporates.) 'Where does a well get its water?' (From groundwater, the water stored in the soil and rock under the ground.) 'Why does water in a clay pot, a matka or mann panai, stay cool?' (Water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside, and evaporation takes heat away.) Say: 'This time we follow water all the way round the world: sea, air, cloud, rain, river and back to the sea.'

steps.title: Story: What the River Remembers
steps.do: Read the story aloud without explaining it. Then ask: 'Why did the river dry up in summer?' and 'What did Pavitra find in the sacred grove?' Write down your child's answers. You will come back to them on Day 4.

steps.title: The bucket and the teaspoon
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Fill a bucket with 10 litres of water, using a 1-litre bottle 10 times. Say: 'This bucket is all the water on Earth.' Take out one glass, about 250 ml. Say: 'This glass is all the fresh water. The rest of the bucket is salty sea.' Pour about two-thirds of the glass into a bowl and put it in the freezer: that is the fresh water frozen in ice and glaciers. Pour most of what is left into a cup of sand: that is groundwater. About half a teaspoon is left in the glass. Say: 'This is all the water in every lake, river and cloud, and inside every living being.' Ask: 'What surprised you?' Then ask: 'Why can't we just drink sea water?' Wait for a guess. Then explain: 'Our kidneys need extra water to get rid of salt. Sea water is so salty that drinking it makes us lose more water than we drink.'

steps.title: Set up: make salt like the salt pans
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1. Stir two spoons of salt into half a glass of water. Pour a thin layer onto a dark plate and put it in the sun, on a window sill or the balcony. Ask: 'When the water has gone, will anything be left on the plate? Why do you think so?' Then say: 'Most of India's salt is made this way, in huge shallow pans of sea water in Gujarat and near Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu.'

need: a glass, a bowl, a cup of sand, a teaspoon

days.title: Ice, water, vapour
days.goal: See water change between its three forms, and find out what a cloud really is.

steps.title: Salt plate
steps.do: Look at the salt plate from Experiment e1. Ask: 'Where did the water go? Why didn't the salt go with it?' (The water evaporated into the air. Salt does not evaporate, so it stayed behind. This is why the sea is salty but rain is fresh.)

steps.title: The sweating steel glass
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Wipe a steel glass dry, then fill it with ice and a little water, and stir in a spoon of salt. Ask: 'Will the outside of the glass get wet? If it does, will that water taste salty?' Wait 5 minutes. Ask: 'Where did the drops come from? Did they leak through the steel?' (No. Air holds water vapour, which is water as an invisible gas. When the vapour touched the cold glass, it cooled and turned back into liquid drops. This is called condensation.) Your child tastes a drop from the outside with a clean finger. It is not salty, because it came from the air, not from inside the glass.

steps.title: A cloud in a bottle
steps.do: Do Experiment e8. First, your child breathes on a cold steel spoon. Ask: 'What made the mist?' (Water vapour in your breath condensed on the cold spoon.) Then pour a little warm water into a clear plastic bottle. A grown-up blows out a lit incense stick, lets a little smoke into the bottle and caps it. Your child squeezes the bottle hard for a few seconds, then lets go. In a dim room, shine a torch through the bottle. Ask: 'When did the cloud appear?' (When you let go.) Try a second bottle with no smoke: the cloud is much fainter. Explain: 'Letting go cools the air a little, and the vapour condenses onto the tiny specks of smoke. Clouds are made of tiny drops of liquid water, not vapour. Vapour itself is invisible.'

steps.title: Set up: a water cycle in a bag
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3. Put four spoons of water and a drop of blue food colour into a zip bag. With a marker, draw the sun, a cloud, a hill and the sea on the bag, with the sea at the bottom. Seal the bag and tape it to a sunny window. Ask: 'What do you think will happen by tomorrow? Why?'

steps.title: Forms hunt
steps.do: Make a chart with three columns: solid, liquid and gas. Walk round the house and find water in each form: ice in the freezer, frost on the freezer wall, tap water, sweat, the white mist above hot tea (tiny liquid drops), and a wet cloth drying (water leaving as invisible vapour). Write each one in its column. Then write the four changes and what each means: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation (liquid to gas) and condensation (gas to liquid).

need: a steel glass, ice and salt
a clear plastic bottle with a cap, warm water, an incense stick and matches (grown-up), a torch
a zip bag, blue food colour, a marker and tape

days.title: The water cycle, and water from leaves
days.goal: Read the water cycle bag, catch water leaving a plant, and hear how people found out where rivers get their water.

steps.title: Read the bag
steps.do: Look at Experiment e3. Ask: 'What happened at the top of the bag? Where did the drops come from? What colour are they?' (The sun warmed the water and it evaporated. The vapour cooled on the plastic at the top and condensed into clear drops, like a cloud. Big drops ran down, like rain, into the sea at the bottom. The blue colour stayed behind, like salt in the sea.) Say: 'No water got into the bag and none got out. It just went round and round. Earth's water does the same.'

steps.title: Water leaving a plant's leaves
steps.do: Look at Experiment e4, which you set up this morning on a potted plant. Ask: 'Do you think there is water inside the bag? Where could it come from?' Untie the bag carefully and look at the drops inside. Ask: 'It did not rain inside the bag. So where did this water come from?' (The plant took up water through their roots. The water went up the stem and out through tiny holes in the leaves, called stomata, as vapour. This is called transpiration.) Say: 'A big tree can give off hundreds of litres of water on a hot day. Over a large forest, a good part of the rain is water that the trees gave off.'

steps.title: Draw and dance the whole cycle
steps.do: First, act out the cycle for 3 minutes. Your child curls up on the floor as sea water. When you say 'sun', they rise slowly as invisible vapour, float as a cloud, curl into a tight ball as a raindrop, jump down, and flow along the floor back to the sea. Then your child draws the water cycle on a big sheet. Include the sea, the sun, evaporation, a cloud (condensation), rain (precipitation), a tree giving off water (transpiration), rain soaking into the ground (infiltration) to become groundwater, a well, and a river running back to the sea. Ask: 'Where does the cycle start?' (It has no start. Each part is fed by the one before it.) Say: 'Earth's water has been going round like this for about four billion years. Some of the water in your glass may once have been inside a dinosaur.'

steps.title: Where do rivers come from?
steps.do: Talk about Voice v1, Palissy and Perrault. First ask: 'Rivers keep flowing for months when there is no rain. Where do you think their water comes from?' Wait for a guess and a reason. Then tell the story. For a long time, many learned people thought rain was too little to feed rivers. A potter, Bernard Palissy, said rivers come from rain soaking into the ground. About a hundred years later, Pierre Perrault measured the rain and the river and showed that Palissy was right. Then ask the voice question.

need: the bag on the potted plant from this morning
a big sheet of paper and colours

prep.task: Tie a clear plastic bag tightly over a leafy branch of a potted plant in the sun, such as tulsi or a money plant. Leave the branch on the plant.

days.title: Water under our feet
days.goal: Measure which ground drinks rain, and see how villages brought their wells back.

steps.title: Which ground drinks the rain?
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. A grown-up cuts four plastic bottles in half. Turn each top half upside down into its bottom half, like a funnel, with a piece of cloth in the neck. Fill each funnel with the same amount of ground: 1, sand; 2, soil from a plant pot; 3, the same pot soil pressed down hard with your fist; 4, pot soil with a layer of dry leaves on top. Ask: 'Which will soak up water fastest? Which will let the most through? Why?' Pour one cup of water on each at the same time. Time how long until no water is left on top, and measure how much drips through in 5 minutes. Write the results in a table. Ask: 'Which ground would fill a well best? Which would flood a road?'

steps.title: Too many straws in one glass
steps.do: Remind your child of the jar well from Class 3, where water seeped in from the soil all around. Say: 'India pumps up more groundwater than any other country. In many parts of Punjab and Haryana, the water under the ground is going down year after year, because more is pumped out than the rain puts back.' Draw a glass with five straws in it. Ask: 'If everyone drinks at once, whose straw stops getting water first, the long straw or the short one?' (The short one. In the same way, families with shallow wells, often the poorer families, lose their water first.) Then say: 'In June 2019, the four big lakes that supply Chennai nearly dried up, and water had to be brought to the city by train.'

steps.title: The johads of Alwar
steps.do: Talk about Voice v2, Rajendra Singh and the villagers of Alwar in Rajasthan. Explain that a johad is a curved bank of earth that holds rainwater so it can soak into the ground. Then look at the story answers you wrote on Day 1. Ask: 'How is a johad like the sacred grove in the story?' (Both slow the rain down so it soaks in. The water then comes out slowly and keeps wells and rivers going in the dry months.) Then ask the voice question.

need: sand, soil from a plant pot, a handful of dry leaves
a cup, a timer, a measuring cup

days.title: Rivers carve the land
days.goal: Make a river in a tray and follow your own rain to the sea.

steps.title: A river in a tray
steps.do: Do Experiment e6 in the bathroom or on the balcony. Fill a tray with damp sand and soil. Put a few books, wrapped in a plastic bag, under one end to make a slope. Make a small hole in a bottle cap, fill the bottle with water, and hold it upside down at the top end so water trickles out. Ask first: 'What will the water do to the sand?' Watch for 10 minutes. Ask: 'What happens to the sand at the top? Where does it go? What shape forms at the bottom?' (At the top the water cuts a channel by carrying sand away. This is erosion. At the bottom the water slows down and drops the sand, building a fan of new land. This is deposition. A delta forms the same way where a river meets the sea.) Put a few small stones in the river's path and watch it bend around them.

steps.title: Which sea does our rain go to?
steps.do: Look at a map of India together, in an atlas or on a phone. Find your town and the nearest river, and follow the river to the sea. Ask: 'Does our rain end up in the Bay of Bengal or the Arabian Sea?' Then show your child that the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri all begin in the Western Ghats, close to the Arabian Sea, but flow east to the Bay of Bengal. Ask: 'Why do they go the long way?' (The land of the Deccan slopes down towards the east, and water always flows downhill.) Explain: 'All the land whose rain drains into one river is called that river's basin. The Ganga's basin covers about a quarter of India.'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 on forms of water, the water cycle and rivers. Read each question aloud if needed. For the two written questions, ask your child to use the salt plate and the water cycle drawing as evidence.

need: a tray or a cut cardboard box lined with plastic
a few books in a plastic bag
a bottle with a pierced cap
an atlas or a map on a phone

days.title: Life in fresh water
days.goal: Watch a pond, test a leaf that stays dry, and build a pond food chain.

steps.title: Pond watch
steps.do: If you can, visit a pond, a lake edge or a temple tank with a grown-up. If there is none nearby, watch a short video of a pond instead. Sit quietly for 10 minutes and list every living being you see: plants floating on the water, plants rooted at the edge, insects walking on the surface (water striders), tiny creatures wriggling just under the surface (mosquito larvae), fish, frogs, snails and birds. Ask: 'Who lives on the surface, who in the water, who at the bottom, and who at the edge?'

steps.title: Listening under water
steps.do: Back home, fill a bucket with water. Your child presses one ear against the side of the bucket. Tap two steel spoons together under the water, then tap them in the air just as hard. Ask: 'Which sounded louder and clearer?' (Under the water. Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and it carries well. Fish and frogs use sound a lot. The Ganga river dolphin, who can hardly see, finds food by making clicks and listening for the echoes.)

steps.title: Why doesn't a lotus leaf get wet?
steps.do: Do Experiment e7 with a lotus leaf or a colocasia leaf (chembu or arbi, sold with the vegetables). First say: 'A lotus leaf lies flat on the water and takes in air through tiny holes on its top side. If water spread over the leaf, it would cover those holes, and dirt would build up.' Ask: 'How do you think the leaf stays dry?' Sprinkle a little dust on the leaf and drip water on it. Watch the drops roll off as balls and pick up the dust. Compare with plain paper, and with paper rubbed hard with a candle. Explain: 'The leaf is covered in tiny bumps coated with wax, so water cannot spread. Engineers copy this to make paint and glass that clean themselves in the rain.'

steps.title: Who eats whom in the pond?
steps.do: Build a pond food chain from your list, with arrows. Explain: 'The arrow means "is eaten by".' Write: algae → mosquito larvae → dragonfly nymphs → small fish → a kingfisher. Say: 'Algae are tiny green living beings. Algae and water plants are called producers, because they make their own food from sunlight.' Add more chains: water plants → snails → ducks, and insects → frogs → a heron or a snake. Join the chains into a food web. Ask: 'What would happen if all the frogs were caught?' (More insects such as mosquitoes, and less food for herons and snakes.) Ask: 'Why do so many land animals live near water too?' (They need water to drink, and water brings food.)

need: a bucket of water and two steel spoons
a lotus or colocasia leaf, a pinch of dust, a candle, paper

days.title: Hidden water and who it belongs to
days.goal: Find the water hidden in food and clothes, play the water game, and wonder where all Earth's water came from.

steps.title: The hidden water hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Say: 'Growing food and making things uses water too. Scientists have worked out rough amounts, which change a lot from place to place.' Share three: one cup of tea, about 30 litres (to grow the tea leaves); one kilogram of rice, about 2,500 litres; one cotton T-shirt, about 2,700 litres. Your child picks five things in the house and guesses which needed the most water. Ask: 'When India sells rice to other countries, what else is it sending away?' (The water used to grow it.)

steps.title: Drama: the Sea and the Sky argue
steps.do: Your child plays the Arabian Sea and you play the land of India in May. Then swap. The Sea says: 'Your rain comes from my water.' The Land says: 'In May I get very hot. The air over me rises, and the wet wind from the sea blows in to take its place. That wind brings the rain.' Say: 'The monsoon wind reaches Kerala first, around the first of June.' Your child adds one more character: the Western Ghats, where the wet wind rises, cools and drops heavy rain.

steps.title: Water's Many Lives card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1. A player turns over a card that names a place or a change, says what happens to that water next, and names the change. Play two rounds, then lay all the cards out and join them into one big water cycle.

steps.title: Where did Earth's water come from?
steps.do: Talk about Voice v3. Say: 'The amount of water on Earth stays about the same.' Ask: 'So where did all of it come from in the first place?' Wait for guesses. Then explain the three ideas: icy comets crashed into the young Earth; or water-rich rocks from space, called asteroids, did; or the rocks that built the Earth already held the water. Ask the voice question. Say: 'Scientists still do not agree.'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Your child uses this week's ideas on new cases: foggy glasses, a city built over its lakes, and the pond creatures from Day 6. Read the questions aloud if needed.

days.title: Design a water-wise home
days.goal: Build a model of a home that catches its own rain, and tackle the challenge worksheet.

steps.title: Rain-harvest model
steps.do: Start the project. Your child builds a house that catches rain: a shoebox for the house, folded cardboard for a sloping roof, half a straw or a cut pipe for the gutter, a cut bottle top with cloth and sand as a filter, and a plastic bottle as the tank. Add a recharge pit: a cup of small stones buried in a tray of soil, where the extra water goes. Pour a mug of water on the roof, follow where it goes and fix any leaks. Say: 'Since 2003, every building in Tamil Nadu must collect rainwater like this.' Ask: 'Our roof is 50 square metres. If 10 millimetres of rain falls, how much water could it catch?' (Every square metre catches 1 litre for each millimetre of rain. 50 × 10 = 500 litres.)

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single right answer, so ask your child for reasons and evidence from this week's tests.

need: a plastic bottle, cloth, sand, small stones

days.title: Check and teach it back
days.goal: Present the water-wise home, answer the check questions and teach the whole cycle back.

steps.title: Present the water-wise home
steps.do: Your child shows the family the model and explains where each drop goes: roof, gutter, filter, tank, overflow and recharge pit. Ask: 'If we had no tank and a cement yard, where would this rain go?' (Into the drain. None would soak in to refill the groundwater.)

steps.title: Check questions
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud, one at a time. Let your child point at the water cycle drawing to explain, and ask 'Why?' after each answer.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches the water cycle to a family member using the drawing from Day 3, and must include: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration, infiltration, a river and the sea. The listener asks one hard question: 'Where does it start?'

steps.title: Who does a river belong to?
steps.do: Say: 'In 2017, New Zealand's Parliament made the Whanganui River a legal person with its own rights, after a long struggle by the Māori people who live along it. In the same year, a high court in India said the Ganga and Yamuna were living beings with rights, but the Supreme Court later put that on hold.' Ask: 'Should a river have rights? Who would speak for the river?' Let your child argue for one side, then the other.

need: the model and the water cycle drawing

experiments.title: Make salt like the salt pans
experiments.question: When salty water evaporates, does the salt go too?
steps: Stir the salt into the water until it disappears.
Pour a thin layer onto the plate.
Leave it in the sun for a day.
Look at it with a magnifying glass if you have one.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When the water has gone, will anything be left?'
experiments.observe: White salt crystals are left on the plate.
experiments.why: Only the water evaporates. Salt can't turn into a gas at this temperature, so it is left behind. This is why the sea is salty and rain is fresh: the sun lifts pure water out of the sea and leaves the salt. Rivers have been carrying tiny amounts of salt from rocks into the sea for millions of years.
experiments.safety: Wash hands after touching the salt water.
experiments.time: 5 min + a day in the sun

experiments.title: The sweating steel glass
experiments.question: Where do the drops on a cold glass come from?
steps: Wipe the glass dry.
Fill it with ice and a little water (add salt if you like).
Wait 5 minutes.
Touch and look at the outside.
Taste a drop from the outside.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the outside get wet? Will it taste of salt?'
experiments.observe: Drops form all over the outside. They are not salty.
experiments.why: Air always holds invisible water vapour. When it touches the cold glass it cools and turns back into liquid: condensation. The drops came from the air, not from inside, so they don't taste of what's inside. Dew on grass forms the same way on cool nights.
experiments.safety: Taste only with a clean finger.

experiments.title: A water cycle in a bag
experiments.question: Can we watch the water cycle happen?
steps: Draw a sun, a cloud, a hill and a sea on the bag.
Put a few spoons of coloured water in the bottom.
Seal it and tape it to a sunny window.
Check after a few hours and the next day.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the water in the sun?'
experiments.observe: Mist and drops gather at the top of the bag, grow, and run down the sides back to the bottom. The drops at the top are clear, not blue.
experiments.why: Sunlight warms the water so it evaporates. The vapour cools on the plastic and condenses into drops, like a cloud. When the drops get heavy they run down, like rain, back to the sea. The colour stays behind, just like salt. No water enters or leaves the bag. It just goes round, the way Earth's water does.

experiments.title: Water leaving a plant's leaves
experiments.question: Do plants put water into the air?
need: a leafy potted plant in the sun
steps: In the morning, put the bag over a leafy branch of the potted plant.
Tie it tightly round the stem.
Leave it in the sun for a few hours.
Untie it carefully and look inside.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will there be water inside the bag? Where could it come from?'
experiments.observe: Drops and mist inside the bag.
experiments.why: A plant takes up water through their roots. Most of that water leaves as vapour through tiny holes in the leaves, called stomata. This is transpiration. As water leaves the leaves, more is drawn up the stem, which is how water reaches the top of a tall tree. Over big forests such as the Amazon, a large part of the rain is water that trees gave off, so cutting forests can mean less rain.
experiments.safety: Use a healthy plant and take the bag off the same day, so the leaves do not overheat.

experiments.title: Which ground drinks the rain?
experiments.question: Which kind of ground lets rain soak in best?
steps: A grown-up cuts each bottle in two. Turn the top half upside down into the bottom half.
Put a piece of cloth in each neck.
Fill the tops with the same amount of: sand, pot soil, pot soil pressed down hard, and pot soil with dry leaves on top.
Pour one cup of water on each at the same time.
Time how long until no water is left on top.
Measure how much drips through in 5 minutes.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will soak up the water fastest? Which will let the most through?'
experiments.observe: Sand drains fastest. Pot soil with leaves on top soaks the water in well and holds some. The pressed-down soil keeps water sitting on top the longest.
experiments.why: Water soaks in through the gaps between grains. Sand has big gaps. Pressing soil squeezes the gaps shut. Leaves and roots slow the water down and keep the soil open, so more soaks in instead of running off. That is how forests and grass refill groundwater, and why trampled or paved ground floods.

experiments.title: A river in a tray
experiments.question: How does flowing water change the shape of the land?
need: a few books in a plastic bag
a bottle with a small hole in the cap
steps: Fill the tray with damp sand and soil and smooth it.
Put the books under one end to make a slope.
Let water trickle from the bottle at the top end.
Watch for 10 minutes and draw what you see.
Add small stones in the path and watch again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the water do to the sand?'
experiments.observe: A channel is cut at the top, the river bends round stones and wanders, and a fan of sand builds up at the bottom.
experiments.why: Moving water picks up soil and sand and carries it away. This is erosion. When the water slows down, at the bottom of a slope or where it meets the sea, it drops the sand. This is deposition. Over thousands of years this carves valleys, like the deep gorges of the Himalaya, and builds deltas, like the Kaveri delta around Thanjavur and the huge Ganga–Brahmaputra delta in Bengal.
experiments.safety: Do it in the bathroom or on the balcony. Wash hands after.

experiments.title: A cloud in a bottle
experiments.question: What does water vapour need to turn into a cloud?
need: a clear plastic bottle with a cap
an incense stick and matches (grown-up only)
steps: Pour a little warm water into the bottle and swirl it.
A grown-up lights the incense stick, blows it out and lets a wisp of smoke into the bottle.
Cap it tightly.
Squeeze the bottle hard for a few seconds, then let go quickly.
In a dim room, shine a torch through the bottle and watch for a cloud. Squeeze again and watch it disappear.
Try again with a fresh bottle and no smoke and compare.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will a cloud appear when I squeeze, or when I let go? Does the smoke matter?'
experiments.observe: A misty cloud appears when you let go and clears when you squeeze. Without smoke it is much fainter.
experiments.why: Letting go lets the air expand and cool, so vapour condenses. But vapour needs something to condense on: tiny specks of dust, smoke or sea salt. Every cloud drop forms around such a speck. That is one reason smoke and dust from cities can change clouds and rain.
experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the match and incense. Do it on a steel plate away from curtains.

experiments.title: Why doesn't a lotus leaf get wet?
experiments.question: How does a lotus keep their floating leaves dry?
need: a dropper or spoon of water
steps: Sprinkle a little dust on the leaf.
Drip water on it and tilt it.
Drip water on plain paper.
Rub a candle hard over another paper and drip water on it.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will get wet? What will happen to the dust?'
experiments.observe: Water forms round balls on the leaf and rolls off, picking up dust. Plain paper soaks; waxed paper beads a little.
experiments.why: A lotus leaf floats on the water and takes in air through tiny holes, called stomata, on its top side. If water covered the leaf, those holes would be blocked and dirt would build up. The leaf is covered in tiny bumps topped with wax, so a drop touches almost nothing and cannot spread. It rolls off and carries the dust away. The German botanist Wilhelm Barthlott studied this from the 1970s and named it the 'lotus effect'.

activities.title: The bucket and the teaspoon
steps: Fill the bucket with 10 litres: all Earth's water.
Take out one glass (250 ml): all the fresh water.
Pour about two-thirds of the glass into a bowl for the freezer: ice caps and glaciers.
Pour most of the rest into the sand: groundwater.
What's left, about half a teaspoon: every lake, river, swamp and cloud and all living things.
Ask: 'Which part of the water can people reach and use easily?'
activities.outcome: A picture your child won't forget of how little fresh water is easy to reach.

activities.title: The hidden water hunt
steps: Learn three rough numbers: cup of tea about 30 litres, 1 kg rice about 2,500 litres, a cotton T-shirt about 2,700 litres.
Pick five things in the house.
Guess and rank them from least to most hidden water.
Talk about what would change if we wasted less food or bought fewer clothes.
activities.outcome: A ranked list of hidden water in your home.

voices.who: Bernard Palissy (about 1510–1590) and Pierre Perrault (1611–1680), France
voices.idea: For about two thousand years, many learned people believed rain was far too little to keep rivers running all year, and that springs were fed by sea water rising through underground passages, or by air turning into water inside mountains. Palissy, a potter with no university education, wrote in 1580 that springs and rivers come only from rain that soaks into the ground. About a hundred years later, Perrault, a lawyer, measured the rain falling on the upper part of the Seine river for three years and compared it with the river's flow. In 1674 he showed that the rain was about six times more than the river carried.
voices.then: Palissy wrote in everyday French, not Latin, and scholars took little notice; he was later imprisoned for his religion and died in the Bastille prison in Paris. Perrault's measurements were quickly checked and supported by Edme Mariotte, and Edmond Halley in England showed that the sun evaporates enough water from the sea to supply all the rain.
voices.now: Accepted. This was one of the first times anyone used measurements to understand the water cycle. Perrault's work is often called the beginning of hydrology, the science of water.
voices.ask: Palissy was right, but he had no measurements. Perrault had numbers. Which would convince you more, and why? How could you measure whether rain is enough to feed your nearest river?

voices.who: Rajendra Singh (born 1959), Tarun Bharat Sangh and the villagers of Alwar, Rajasthan, India
voices.idea: In 1985 Rajendra Singh came to the dry Alwar district. Village elders told him the real problem was not illness but water: the wells were dry and the forests on the hills had been cut. With the villagers, especially women, he helped rebuild johads, curved earth banks that hold rainwater so it soaks into the ground. Over the next years villages built thousands of them. Wells filled again, and the Arvari river, which had stopped flowing in the dry season, began flowing all year. The villages set up the Arvari River Parliament to share its water fairly.
voices.then: At first some officials said the johads were built without permission. Many engineers thought small earth banks could not matter compared with big dams.
voices.now: Accepted that the johads raised groundwater and brought rivers back; Rajendra Singh won the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015. Scientists still study how much of the change came from the johads and how much from rainy years, and they warn that too many small dams upstream can leave less water for villages downstream.
voices.ask: Villagers in Rajasthan had built johads for hundreds of years, but many engineers trusted only big dams. What would you measure to find out whether johads really work?

voices.who: Where did Earth's water come from? Comets, asteroids, or Earth's own rocks (the Rosetta comet mission, 2014, and Laurette Piani and colleagues, 2020)
voices.idea: One idea is that icy comets crashed into the young Earth and brought the oceans. Another is that water-rich asteroids did. A third is that the rocks Earth was built from already held enough water. In 2020 Laurette Piani and her team, studying meteorites similar to the stuff Earth formed from, found they hold enough hydrogen to have made several oceans' worth of water.
voices.then: In 2014 the European spacecraft Rosetta tasted the water of comet 67P and found it had much more 'heavy' hydrogen than Earth's oceans, so comets like that one probably didn't bring most of our water.
voices.now: Debated. Most scientists think asteroids or Earth's own rocks, or a mix, gave us most of our water, but there is no agreement. Some studies also suggest that part of the water on Earth is older than the Sun itself.
voices.ask: Scientists compared the 'fingerprint' of comet water and sea water. What other clue would help you decide where our water came from?

project.title: A water-wise home
steps: Build a shoebox house with a sloping cardboard roof.
Add a gutter from a cut straw or half a pipe.
Make a filter from a bottle top with cloth and sand.
Use a plastic bottle as the storage tank.
Add an overflow to a recharge pit (a cup of gravel buried in a tray of soil).
Test it with a mug of 'rain' and fix leaks.
Work out how many litres your real roof could catch in a 10 mm rain (roof area in square metres × 10).
Present the model to the family and explain every drop's path.
project.outcome: A working rain-harvesting model and a calculation for your own home.

game.title: Water's Many Lives
rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
Take turns to turn one over and read the front aloud.
Say what happens to the water next, and name the change if there is one (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration, infiltration, melting, freezing).
Check the back. A right answer with the right word scores 2 points; right idea without the word scores 1.
When all cards are used, the highest score wins. Then lay all the cards out and join them into one big water cycle.

cards.front: A puddle on a hot afternoon
cards.back: Evaporates into the air as water vapour

cards.front: Warm, wet air rising up a mountain
cards.back: Cools and condenses into cloud drops

cards.front: Cloud drops bumping and growing heavy
cards.back: Fall as rain: precipitation
Soaks in: infiltration, then groundwater
Runs off into a drain and a river

cards.front: A neem tree on a sunny day
cards.back: Gives off water from its leaves: transpiration

cards.front: Snow on a Himalayan peak in spring
cards.back: Melts and flows into a river
Drops its mud (a delta) and joins the salty sea

cards.front: The sea under the hot sun
cards.back: Evaporates; the salt stays behind

cards.front: A cold steel glass on a humid day
cards.back: Vapour condenses into drops on the outside
Freezes into ice
Seeps out as a spring or into a well
Holds water so it soaks in and recharges wells
Leaves as breath, sweat and urine, back to the cycle
Can stay frozen for thousands of years, then melt
Formed by condensation; evaporates when the sun rises
Takes groundwater faster than rain may refill it

cards.front: Rain on a rooftop with a gutter and tank
cards.back: Collected and stored: rain harvesting
Invisible vapour, then a white mist of tiny drops

cards.front: A drop in a pond with a lotus
cards.back: May be taken up by the lotus's roots and given off from the leaves
Ice; melts into water on the ground

cards.front: A drop you drank this morning
cards.back: Has been round the cycle for billions of years
Name three places that water could be today
Invent a water journey with three changes

story.title: What the River Remembers
text: I am a small river. You will not find me on most maps. I begin in the hills of Kodagu in Karnataka, and I run for only forty kilometres before I join a bigger river. That river joins the Kaveri, and after many days the Kaveri reaches the Bay of Bengal. That is where I came from in the first place, though nobody in the villages along my banks would believe it.

I remember everything. I remember being sea, warm and green and salty, rocking under the sun. I remember being lifted, one invisible piece at a time, leaving my salt behind, rising so high that the air turned cold and I gathered myself into a cloud. I remember being blown by the monsoon wind across the land, and falling. I have done this many thousands of times. Once, a long time ago, I was ice. Once I was inside an elephant. Once, I think, inside a dinosaur. Water does not get used up. It only moves.

Two villages live along me. Up in the hills is Malehalli, with its coffee bushes, its rice fields and its small temple in a grove of old trees. Down in the plain is Holedande, where the fields are wide and flat and people grow vegetables to sell in the town.

For as long as anyone remembered, I flowed all year. In the monsoon I was wide and brown and loud. In the dry months, from January to May, I was thin and clear and quiet, but I never stopped. The women of Holedande washed clothes on my stones in April. The buffaloes stood in me up to their bellies in May. A kingfisher lived in a hole in my bank and fished in me every single day.

Then, over a few years, things changed. The hills above Malehalli had been covered with forest. People needed firewood, a contractor came with saws, and the slopes were cleared for fields and for timber. When the monsoon came, I was no longer just wide and brown. I was wild. The rain hit the bare slopes and raced straight down into me, carrying the red soil with it, and I flooded the fields of Holedande and drowned the young plants. And then, by February, I was gone. Just dry stones, a smell of mud, and the kingfisher sitting on a dead branch.
In Holedande people were angry. 'Malehalli is taking our river,' they said. 'They must have built a dam up there. They must be pumping it all out.'

A girl called Pavitra, who was ten, decided to find out for herself. One morning in March, with her cousin, a bottle of water and a packet of chikki, she walked up my dry bed towards the hills. It took most of the day. She saw no dam. She saw no pumps. The people of Malehalli were as worried as hers: their own wells were low, and their own fields were cracking. A girl called Gowri, who was looking after her family's goats, walked with her the last part of the way.
'There's no dam,' Gowri said. 'The river just stops. Come and see.'

They climbed to where I begin. There was nothing there, just a gully of bare red rock, dry as a brick, with a few thorny bushes. Pavitra sat down on a stone and nearly cried. Where was the river? Where had all that water gone, the water that once flowed all year?
'There's one more place,' said Gowri. 'The devara kadu, the sacred grove. Nobody cuts the trees there. It belongs to the god.'

The grove was a small patch of forest around the old temple, a few hundred trees that nobody had touched for hundreds of years. Inside it was dark and cool. The ground was soft and deep with fallen leaves, and it gave under their feet like a mattress. There were ferns. There was moss on the roots. And in the deepest part, under a huge old tree whose roots ran down between the stones, there was a sound Pavitra had not heard for months: a trickle.

She knelt and put her hand in it. Cold water was coming out of the ground. Not much, a thin silver thread no wider than her finger, but in March, in a dry year, when every other part of the hill was bare rock and dust, here I was.

Pavitra looked at the soft, deep ground and the thick leaves and the roots. She looked back down at the bare hillside. And she understood something that the people who cut the forest had never thought about. The forest had never made the water. The rain made the water. But the forest held it. The thick leaf litter, the roots and the soft soil caught the monsoon rain and let it sink slowly into the ground. Then, for months afterwards, the water came out again, drop by drop, into me. The forest was where I kept my water between the rains. When the forest went, the rain had nowhere to wait.

It took a long time after that. There were meetings, and arguments, and more arguments. But in the end the hill village and the plain village agreed to work together. They planted trees on the bare slopes, thousands of them. They dug long trenches along the hillside to slow the rain. They let the grass grow back and kept the goats off it for a few years. Gowri and Pavitra planted forty saplings each, and watered them by hand through the first dry season.

I did not come back the next year, or the year after that. Trees grow slowly, and soil grows more slowly still. But in the fourth year, in April, a thin clear thread of me ran past Holedande for the first time in a long while. In the fifth year I reached the bigger river in May.

And this morning, as I write this, the kingfisher dived into me, and came up with a fish, and I felt the small cold splash of it, and thought: I was the sea once. I was a cloud. I will be the sea again. But for these few months, I am this, and I am here.
story.epiphany: The river tells the water cycle from the inside (sea, cloud, rain, river, sea), so the child meets the idea that water is never used up, only moved. The turn comes in the sacred grove: Pavitra sees that the forest does not make water but holds it, letting rain soak in and releasing it slowly as groundwater and springs. Without the forest, rain runs straight off, causing floods and carrying soil away, and the river dries in summer. The two villages blame each other until they see they share one problem. Sacred groves (devara kadu in Kodagu, kaavu in Kerala) are real forests that communities have protected for centuries.
ask: Why did the river flood in the monsoon and then dry up in February?
What did Pavitra understand when she put her hand in the trickle?
The people of Holedande thought Malehalli had taken their river. Were they right? What was really happening?
The sacred grove belonged to the god, so nobody cut the trees. What did that do for the river?
The river says, 'I was the sea once. I will be the sea again.' What does the river mean?

ideas.idea: The water cycle has no beginning and no end, and the same water is used again and again.
ideas.more: Every drop has been sea, cloud, ice and living things many times over. The water cycle bag shows this: nothing enters or leaves, it only goes round.

ideas.idea: Almost all of Earth's water is out of reach.
ideas.more: About 97 drops in every 100 are salty sea, and most of the fresh water is ice or deep underground. The bucket and the teaspoon makes this real.

ideas.idea: Forests and soil are where rivers keep their water.
ideas.more: Leaf litter, roots and soil soak up rain and release it slowly as groundwater and springs. Cut them and you get floods in the monsoon and dry riverbeds in summer.
Every valley, gorge and delta was shaped by flowing water carrying soil from one place to another, grain by grain, over thousands of years.

unknowns: Where did Earth's water come from in the first place: comets, asteroids, or the rocks the Earth was made from? Scientists disagree.

How will a warming world change the Indian monsoon? Scientists have found that very heavy rain days have become more common in central India since the 1950s, but how the whole monsoon will behave in 50 years is still uncertain.

How much water is hidden deep inside the Earth, hundreds of kilometres down in the rocks of the mantle? A tiny crystal found inside a diamond in 2014 suggested there might be as much as in all the oceans, but nobody knows for sure.
big: If water keeps going round and round, why do people say we are running out of it?
Who owns a river that flows through many villages, states or countries?
Should a river have rights, like a person? Who would speak for it?
Would you rather live upstream or downstream? Why?
The water you drink leaves your body as breath, sweat and urine, and goes round the cycle again. Is that water part of you, or just passing through?

challenge.hint: Water vapour is an invisible gas. Clouds and the white mist above a kettle are made of billions of tiny liquid drops (or ice crystals) that have already condensed. You can see them because they scatter light. Ask: if vapour is invisible, how do we know it's in the air? (The sweating glass.)

challenge.q: 'Water is renewable, so we can never run out.'
challenge.hint: The total amount of water on Earth stays the same, but water in one place can run out. Groundwater that took thousands of years to collect can be pumped out in a few decades. Satellites have measured groundwater falling fast under north-west India. Ask: is a bank account 'renewable' if you take out more than you put in?

A spring is only where groundwater comes out of the ground. That groundwater came from rain or melting snow that soaked in earlier. So every river really starts as rain or snow. Palissy and Perrault argued this hundreds of years ago. Ask: where does the water of the Ganga come from in May, when it has not rained for months? (Mostly melting snow and ice, plus groundwater.)

perspectives.view: In this cold desert, farming depends on meltwater from glaciers and snow in spring. If the ice melts too early or too little, fields go dry just when seeds need water. Ask: how is a glacier like a water tank?

The Ganga and Brahmaputra carry mud from the Himalaya and built the islands where they live. Now dams and barrages upstream hold back some of that mud, and the sea is rising. Some islands, such as Ghoramara, are shrinking. Ask: can a dam be good for one place and bad for another?

In 1983 she and the geologist Sudipta Sengupta became the first Indian women to go to Antarctica, with India's third expedition. Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in the ice there. Ask: why would a scientist travel to the coldest place on Earth to study the sea?

A dragonfly spends most of their life, often many months or longer, as a nymph under the water of a pond, hunting tadpoles and larvae. Then they climb a reed, their skin splits, and they fly. Ask: is a dragonfly a water animal or an air animal?

perspectives.who: The village of Hiware Bazar, Maharashtra
perspectives.view: After years of drought, the villagers built check dams and planted trees, and now they measure their water every year after the monsoon and decide together which crops to grow so they don't take more than the rain gives. Ask: what would a 'water budget' for your home look like?

perspectives.who: A rice farmer in the Kaveri delta, Tamil Nadu
perspectives.view: The Kaveri begins in Kodagu in Karnataka. Dams upstream in Karnataka store its water, and farmers around Thanjavur, far downstream, need that water to grow rice. The two states have argued in courts about sharing it for many years. Ask: if a river flows through two states, how should its water be shared in a dry year?

books.title: A Drop of Water: A Book of Science and Wonder
books.author: Walter Wick
books.why: Astonishing close-up photographs of drops, snowflakes, frost and steam that make evaporation and condensation visible.

books.title: All the Water in the World
books.author: George Ella Lyon (illustrated by Katherine Tillotson)
books.why: A poem about how all the water there is keeps moving round: 'that rain that soaked your hair'.

books.title: The Cloud Book
books.author: Tomie dePaola
books.why: The main kinds of clouds, what they tell you about the weather, and some old cloud sayings to test. Use it with the cloud in a bottle.

books.title: Pond Circle
books.author: Betsy Franco (illustrated by Stefano Vitale)
books.why: A pond food chain told as a rhyme that grows longer on each page. Use it on Day 6.

books.title: Aaj Bhi Khare Hain Talab (The Ponds Are Still Standing)
books.author: Anupam Mishra
books.age: adult book (Hindi; English translations exist); read parts aloud
books.why: The stories of the people who built India's ponds and tanks, and the knowledge they carried.

check.q: If all Earth's water were a bucket, how much would be fresh and easy to reach?
check.a: Fresh water is about one glass; the water in lakes, rivers and the air is only about half a teaspoon.

check.q: What is condensation? Give an example.
check.a: Water vapour cooling and turning into liquid drops, such as drops on a cold glass, dew, or clouds.

check.q: Explain the water cycle using these words: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration, infiltration.
check.a: Sun evaporates water from the sea and land and plants transpire it; it condenses into clouds; falls as precipitation; soaks in by infiltration or runs into rivers back to the sea.

check.q: Why is rain fresh even though most of it comes from the salty sea?
check.a: Only the water evaporates; the salt is left behind.

check.q: How does a river change the land?
check.a: It wears away soil and rock (erosion) and drops it where it slows down (deposition), carving valleys and building deltas.
For example: algae → mosquito larvae → dragonfly nymphs → small fish → kingfisher.

check.q: Why does cutting a forest make a river flood and then dry up?
check.a: Without leaf litter and roots, rain runs straight off instead of soaking in, so there are floods in the rains and no slow supply of groundwater in the dry months.

check.q: Name one way a community can catch and share rain.
check.a: Johads, check dams, rooftop rain harvesting, recharge pits, village water budgets.
